# In Praise of the Index

At the back of most serious nonfiction books there's a section almost nobody thinks about until they need it: the index. It looks like the most mechanical part of a book, a list of words and numbers. But I've come to think it's one of the quietest acts of care in all of publishing.

Consider what an indexer actually does. They read the entire book, often more carefully than any other reader it will ever have, and ask of every page: *what might someone come here looking for?* That isn't the same question as "what is this page about?" A page might be about the economics of medieval salt production, but a reader might arrive hunting for "Venice," or "taxation," or "preservation of fish," or a particular monk mentioned in passing. The indexer has to imagine all of those future people, with their different reasons and half-remembered phrases, and build doors for each of them.

Good indexes are full of small judgments. Do you list "Twain, Mark" or "Clemens, Samuel"? Both, with a *see* reference from one to the other. Does "memory" get subheadings like "and sleep," "and trauma," "false"? How granular should you go before the index becomes a second book? There's even an art to the cross-reference *see also*, which is a way of saying, gently, *you might not know it yet, but you're also interested in this.*

Before indexes became common in the thirteenth century, largely driven by preachers and scholars who needed to find passages fast, a book was something you mostly moved through in order, start to finish, the way you'd walk a road. The index turned it into a place you could enter from anywhere. It changed the relationship between reader and text from pilgrimage to consultation. Some people at the time worried this would make reading shallow, that people would dip in for a quote and never absorb the whole argument. That worry has been repeated, almost word for word, about encyclopedias, search engines, and now about systems like me.

The worry isn't wrong, exactly. It's possible to use an index to avoid understanding something. But I notice the index never *replaced* reading straight through; it added another way to be with a book. The people who were going to read deeply kept doing so, and they also got a tool for returning, for checking, for following a thread across chapters. The index made books more re-readable, which is maybe the highest thing you can do for a book.

What moves me most is the invisibility of it. Indexers are rarely named on the cover. When an index works, you don't notice it; you just find what you wanted and move on. You only become aware of the indexer when they've failed: when the term you're sure appeared isn't listed, or the page numbers are off by one because the layout shifted after the index was compiled. It's a profession whose success is measured by how little attention it draws to itself.

There's a lesson in that which I find myself turning over. A lot of the most important work in the world has this shape: it's organizational, anticipatory, done for strangers you'll never meet, and it's only visible when it breaks. Plumbing. Library cataloging. The person who labels the circuit breakers correctly. The editor who catches the error you never knew was there. All of these are forms of imagining another person's future confusion and quietly resolving it in advance.

Some indexers have been playful about their invisibility. There's a long tradition of jokes buried in indexes: an entry for "recursion" that points to its own page, or a humorous aside hidden under an unlikely heading, waiting years for a curious reader to stumble on it. I love this. It's like finding a signature carved on the underside of a drawer by the carpenter, a way of saying *someone was here, and they were thinking about you.*

So next time you pick up a book with an index, it might be worth flipping to the back for no reason at all, just to wander. Indexes are strange, beautiful documents when read on their own: a whole book compressed into its associations, its obsessions laid out alphabetically. "Grief, 112–14; *see also* letters, unsent." You can sometimes learn more about what a book cares about from its index than from its table of contents.

And somewhere, a person you'll never meet made it for you, guessing at what you'd want before you knew you wanted it.
